written.q: Compare supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning with an example each.
written.a: Supervised: labelled data with correct answers (past exam questions with answers; classification, regression, time series). Unsupervised: unlabelled data, the machine finds groups or relationships (clustering, association rules). Reinforcement: an agent learns by trial and error through rewards and penalties (training a puppy; Boston Dynamics robots).

written.q: Explain how the two-model donor example decides whom to contact. Compute the profit for a donor with probability 0.8, amount 500 and a 25 letter cost.
written.a: Model 1 (classification) predicts whether a person will donate; model 2 (regression) predicts how much. Expected value = probability x amount; contact only if it beats the cost. 0.8 x 500 = 400; 400 - 25 = 375 profit, so contact.

written.q: Explain the curse of dimensionality and how PCA helps.
written.a: As features increase, data becomes sparse (10 levels per feature gives 10^n boxes), distances between points become similar and lose meaning, and models overfit and need heavy computing. PCA creates a few new features keeping most of the variation, reducing dimensions with little information loss.

written.q: Explain bias, variance, underfitting and overfitting and how to diagnose them from training and testing errors.
written.a: High bias (underfitting): too simple, high training and testing error. High variance (overfitting): too flexible, near-zero training error but high testing error. A good model has low error on both. Choosing the right complexity is the bias-variance problem.

For data (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), w = 0, b = 0, learning rate 0.01, perform one gradient descent step.
written.a: Errors 2, 4, 6; SSE 56. Slope for b = -2 x 12 = -24; slope for w = -2 x (2 + 8 + 18) = -56. New b = 0 - 0.01 x (-24) = 0.24; new w = 0.56. SSE falls to about 25.06.

written.q: Explain logistic regression: why a sigmoid, the decision boundary, and how it differs from linear regression.
written.a: A straight line is unbounded and sensitive to outliers; probabilities must lie between 0 and 1. Logistic regression computes z = wx + b and passes it through sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^-z), giving a probability; predict class 1 if it is at least 0.5. The boundary is where z = 0 (a hyperplane). Linear regression predicts a number and is fitted by least squares; logistic regression predicts a probability/category and is fitted by maximum likelihood (or small error with gradient descent).
